rapidFireQAs.q: 70F + healthy + has pulmonary function tests performed as part of a study. In comparison to a healthy woman age 20, what are her arrows (i.e., ↑ or ↓) for FEV1, FVC, and FEV1/FVC?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↓ FEV1, ↓ FVC, ↓ FEV1/FVC. — USMLE wants you to know that people naturally develop obstructive lung disease throughout the course of their lives, likely as a result of lifetime inhalation of particulates. • These arrows are the same for COPD due to smoking, asthma, and a1-antitrypsin deficiency (emphysema). • Knowing the FEV1, FVC, and FEV1/FVC arrows for obstructive vs restrictive lung diseases is mandatory to pass Step 1.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25M + non-smoker + progressively worsening shortness of breath + chest x-ray shows bullous changes; dad died of alcoholic liver disease at age 45. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for residual volume, arterial pO2, and A-a gradient?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↑ residual volume, ↓ arterial pO2, ↑ A-a gradient. — Diagnosis is a1-antitrypsin deficiency. • Classically causes pan-acinar emphysema and cirrhosis of the liver. • a1-antitrypsin is a protease produced in the liver that breaks down elastase in the lungs. Elastase destroys lung tissue. So if a1-antitrypsin is present, there’s less elastase, and less destruction of lung tissue. In this disease (deficiency), we get emphysema due to lung destruction. • “Bullous changes on chest x-ray” = emphysema on USMLE. Emphysema = obstructive lung disease. • Codominant inheritance pattern. Vignettes might give sibling or parent also with lung or liver disease. • Student says, “But dad died of alcoholic liver disease it says, so why is that genetic?” → implication is the father had one or more of the disease alleles, which caused greater susceptibility to accelerated liver disease in the setting of alcohol consumption. (I’ve seen this in NBME vignettes) • Residual volume is increased in obstructive lung diseases and decreased in restrictive. • Arterial pO2 is decreased in both obstructive and restrictive lung diseases. • A-a gradient is increased in both obstructive and restrictive lung diseases, as well as in pulmonary edema. • The key point to remember about A-a gradient is that it is normal (i.e., not elevated) in hypoventilation / ventilatory insufficiency → benzos, barbiturates, opioids → all cause respiratory depression.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate born at 26 weeks’ gestation + respiratory distress. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for pulmonary compliance, pulmonary elastic recoil, pulmonary sphingomyelin, and lamellar body activity?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↓ pulmonary compliance, ↑ elastic recoil, ↑ sphingomyelin, ↓ lamellar body activity. — Diagnosis is neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS), caused by surfactant deficiency. • Compliance = ability to expand. • Elastic recoil = ability to collapse. • Surfactant prevents alveolar collapse by providing a lipophilic lining to the alveolar sacs that decreases hydrostatic collapsing forces. • If surfactant is low, then collapsing forces are greater. Therefore, elastic recoil is up. • If collapsing forces are greater, then ability to expand is less. Therefore, compliance is down. • The lecithin (dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine) : sphingomyelin ratio is high (i.e., >2.0-2.4) when fetal lungs have matured >36 weeks’ gestation. In other words, a high ratio is good; a low ratio is bad. • In NRDS, we expect lecithin (dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine) to be low and sphingomyelin to be up. • Lamellar bodies are specialized organelles within type II pneumocytes that produce surfactant. Activity is reduced when the lungs have not yet matured. (I’ve seen this asked on retired Step 1 NBME)

rapidFireQAs.q: 50M + long history of smoking + COPD. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for mucous production, activity of airway cilia, and alveolar macrophage function?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↑ mucous production, ↓ activity of airway cilia, ↓ alveolar macrophage function. — In COPD, bronchiolar mucous production is increased (increased Reid index ratio). • Cilia function of pseudostratified columnar epithelial cells of the airway is decreased. This is exceedingly HY for USMLE. Students might say, “Wait, but if there are more particulates in the lungs from smoking, wouldn’t cilia function be up to compensate cuz we’re clearing stuff out more?” → apparently particulates/smoking actually impair the cilia function. I’ve also seen NBME ask which cell in a smoker is most impaired, and the answer is “pseudostratified columnar epithelial cell” → implying the ciliated cell of the airways. • Particulates/smoking impair alveolar macrophage function. Similar to the cilia scenario, a student might think there’s increased activity to compensate, but the macrophage function is damaged in the setting of ongoing particulate exposure.

rapidFireQAs.q: 65M + orthopnea + paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure, alveolar interstitial hydrostatic pressure, and alveolar interstitial oncotic pressure?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↑ pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure, ↑ alveolar interstitial hydrostatic pressure, ↓ alveolar interstitial oncotic pressure. — The patient has left heart failure. The backup of pressure from the left heart causes increased pressure in the pulmonary circulation. • Since left atrial pressure (LAP) is up, PCWP must be up. High PCWP means pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure is up. • Hydrostatic pressure = fluid pressure (i.e., lots of fluid/volume in a compartment = higher pressure). • Oncotic pressure = solute pressure (i.e., lots of solutes/proteins in a compartment = higher pressure). • Hydrostatic pressure is an outward pressure (i.e., high hydrostatic pressure in a vessel → more fluid leaves vessel). • Oncotic pressure is a retention pressure (i.e., high oncotic pressure in a vessel → fluid less likely to leave vessel). • High PCWP = high pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure → fluid leaves pulmonary microvasculature for the alveolar spaces → pulmonary edema. • Since we now have fluid in the alveolar spaces, alveolar interstitial hydrostatic pressure must now be higher (i.e., the mere presence of fluid there means there must be a greater hydrostatic pressure). • This fluid that enters the alveolar spaces is transudate, not exudate. Transudate is relatively devoid of proteins, cells, and LDH, and is a result of differences in hydrostatic and oncotic pressures between fluid compartments. Exudate is high in proteins, cells, and LDH, and is the result of an inflammatory process. • Since the fluid in the alveolar spaces is transudate, it is low in protein. So the oncotic pressure it exerts is low. • This combination of arrows for this Q seems a bit unusual but is asked on the Step 1.

rapidFireQAs.q: 55M + long history of systemic hypertension + chest x-ray shows pleural effusion and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates; ECG shows left bundle-branch block. If we are forced to pick high or low values, what are the arrows (i.e., ↑ or ↓) for pleural fluid LDH, pleural fluid protein, and pleural fluid glucose?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↓ Pleural fluid LDH, ↓ pleural fluid protein, ↑ glucose. — Patient has fluid in his lungs due to increased pressures in his left heart secondary to systemic hypertension. • LBBB = left ventricular hypertrophy on USMLE. • The fluid would be transudate because the cause is increased pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure. • Pleural fluid:serum LDH ratio of <0.6 is consistent with transudate; >0.6 is exudate. • Pleural fluid:serum protein ratio <0.5 is transudate; >0.5 is exudate. • In other words, there’s low LDH and protein in transudate. • Low glucose in the pleural fluid signifies bacterial or fungal infection (i.e., glucose is being consumed by the organisms). In this case, we don’t overtly suspect an infection, so if we are forced to choose between an up or down arrow, up makes more sense. • On the USMLE, you will sometimes get columns of numbers in the answer choices, where you’re forced to choose between, e.g., a 20 or 80 mg/dL for glucose. The 20 would be for exudative pleural effusion in the setting of pneumonia. 80 would be for transudate. The concept is: glucose of pleural fluid that “isn’t too far away from” serum glucose is consistent with transudate.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22F + iron deficiency anemia. Compared to individuals without IDA, what are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for arterial pO2, hemoglobin saturation, and arterial O2 content?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↔ Arterial pO2, ↔ hemoglobin saturation, ↓ arterial O2 content. — NBME loves this Q. It’s repeated across forms. • Arterial O2 content = oxygen dissolved in the blood (pO2) + oxygen bound to hemoglobin (Hb-O2). • The pathway for oxygen entering the body is: Inhaled into lungs → moves through capillary walls of alveoli → dissolves in blood as pO2 → hops onto hemoglobin as Hb-O2. • In iron deficiency anemia, there is simply low hemoglobin. There is absolutely nothing wrong with the ability of the lungs to conduct gas exchange, so arterial pO2 is normal. • Since pO2 is normal, the dissolved oxygen hops onto the available hemoglobin, so hemoglobin saturation is normal. Just because hemoglobin is low due to anemia doesn’t mean there is any impairment in the ability of hemoglobin to bind oxygen. • Since we have less hemoglobin, even though hemoglobin saturation is normal, the total quantity of oxygen bound to hemoglobin is therefore decreased. This is why arterial oxygen content is low. • Some students might say, “Well if we have the same oxygen making its way into the blood but we have less hemoglobin, wouldn’t the available hemoglobin have increased saturation then?” → hemoglobin saturation is not increased because Hb is already maximally saturated in the absence of anemia in healthy patients, so it won’t go up anymore.

There is absolutely nothing wrong with the ability of the lungs to conduct gas exchange, so arterial pO2 is normal. • Since pO2 is normal, the dissolved oxygen hops onto the available hemoglobin, so hemoglobin saturation is normal. Just because hemoglobin is low due to anemia doesn’t mean there is any impairment in the ability of hemoglobin to bind oxygen. • Since we have less hemoglobin, even though hemoglobin saturation is normal, the total quantity of oxygen bound to hemoglobin is therefore decreased. This is why arterial oxygen content is low. • Some students might say, “Well if we have the same oxygen making its way into the blood but we have less hemoglobin, wouldn’t the available hemoglobin have increased saturation then?” → hemoglobin saturation is not increased because Hb is already maximally saturated in the absence of anemia in healthy patients, so it won’t go up anymore.

rapidFireQAs.q: Shunt = ↓ V/Q
rapidFireQAs.a: refers to almost all lung conditions on USMLE.

rapidFireQAs.q: Dead space = ↑ V/Q
rapidFireQAs.a: refers to basically just pulmonary embolism on USMLE.

rapidFireQAs.q: ↓ V/Q can also refer to the physiologic (i.e., normal) shunt we see at the lung bases, where V/Q is 0.6. This is because despite both ventilation and perfusion ↑ apex
rapidFireQAs.a: base, gravity pulls blood down more greatly than air, so perfusion ↑↑ toward the bases, whereas ventilation only ↑. So V/Q is ↓ at the bases (shunt).

rapidFireQAs.q: But the above needs to be taken with a caveat. For example, the Q might say the patient is on a ventilator and has arterial pO2 of 40 mm Hg (normal is 80-100) + FiO2 is 100% + tidal volume is 1000 mL, and the answer will be “increase PEEP.” The student says, “Wait but I thought you said we want to reduce FiO2 and tidal volume.”
rapidFireQAs.a: Sure, but we can’t do that here because pO2 is super-low, so that would only exacerbate it further.

rapidFireQAs.q: They also ask the inverse of this on NBME – i.e., they say an anesthesiologist wants to ↑ a patient’s cerebral perfusion, and the answer is “decrease respiratory rate”
rapidFireQAs.a: causes ↑ CO2 → ↑ cerebral perfusion.

rapidFireQAs.q: Patients should ideally be weaned from ventilators as quickly as possible. USMLE also likes patients who are sick on ventilators as sometimes having euthyroid sick syndrome – i.e., they will say patient cannot be weaned from ventilator + has ↓ T3 and normal TSH
rapidFireQAs.a: euthyroid sick syndrome. The full array of arrows are: ↓ T3, ↑ rT3, ↔ T4, ↔ TSH. If you have no idea what I’m talking about, then I recommend going through my HY Arrows PDF.

rapidFireQAs.q: 58F + 6-month Hx of shortness of breath and non-productive cough + 2-year Hx of worsening dysphagia + 20-yr Hx of hands turning white when exposed to cold; what lung condition is this patient most at risk of developing?
rapidFireQAs.a: pulmonary hypertension → pulmonary fibrosis common in CREST syndrome (scleroderma; limited systemic sclerosis) → pulmonary fibrosis seen in both diffuse and limited types of systemic sclerosis; the latter is sans the renal phenomena) → can lead to cor pulmonale, which is right-heart failure secondary to a pathology of lung etiology (i.e., the left heart must not be causative).

rapidFireQAs.q: What will the USMLE frequently say in the Q if they’re hinting at pulmonary hypertension?
rapidFireQAs.a: HY vignette descriptors are loud S2 or P2 (pulmonic valve slams shut when the distal pressure is high); dilation of proximal pulmonary arteries; increased pulmonary vascular markings (congestion + increased hydrostatic pressure).

rapidFireQAs.q: When is “pulmonary hypertension” important as the answer? → notably in Eisenmenger syndrome and cor pulmonale.
rapidFireQAs.a: Regarding Eisenmenger: the reversal of the L-to-R shunt across the VSD such that it’s R-to-L requires the tunica media of the pulmonary arterioles to hypertrophy secondary to chronic increased preload → proximal backup of hydrostatic pressure → increased afterload on the right heart → now the right heart starts to significantly hypertrophy → shunt across the VSD reverses R-to-L. This is important, as RVH is not the most upstream cause of Eisenmenger; the pulmonary hypertension is. Regarding cor pulmonale: as mentioned above, cor pulmonale is right heart failure secondary to a pathology of pulmonary etiology (e.g., COPD, cystic fibrosis [CF], fibrosis, etc.). The most common cause of right heart failure is left heart failure, so for cor pulmonale to be the diagnosis, the left heart must not be the etiology of the right heart failure; the lungs must be the etiology. Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) must be normal. If the cause of the right heart failure is, e.g., chronic bronchitis or CF, then it is the degree of hypoxic vasoconstriction that determines the prognosis for the cor pulmonale. For chronic bronchitis and CF --> hypoxic vasoconstriction of pulmonary vessels --> increased afterload in the proximal pulmonary arteries --> dilatation and congestion of proximal pulmonary arteries --> more hydrostatic pressure in the proximal pulmonary arteries --> increased afterload experienced by the right heart --> right heart hypertrophies --> right heart eventually decompensates secondary to chronically elevated pulmonary vascular pressure --> classic right heart failure signs ensue (JVD + pulmonary edema; hepatosplenomegaly may also be seen [e.g., spleen tip and/or liver edge are palpable beneath the costal margin]).For emphysema, loss of alveolar surface area --> loss of capillary surface area --> increase in pulmonary vascular resistance (decreased # of capillaries forming parallel circuit) --> pulmonary hypertension --> increased afterload on right ventricle --> cor pulmonale.

rapidFireQAs.q: “Please explain PCWP. I’ve seen that before but no idea what that means or how it applies to questions.” → If you stick a catheter into the venous circulation and feed it all the way back up to the right heart and into the pulmonary circulation, eventually it won’t be able to go and farther and will be lodged in a distal pulmonary arteriole; the pressure reverberations sensed by the catheter must therefore reflect the pulmonary capillary pressure (immediately distal to the catheter); but of course the pulmonary capillary pressure must reflect the left atrial pressure because the latter is immediately contiguous; therefore PCWP = left atrial pressure. This is a very simple rule that must be memorized and understood for the USMLE. For the purpose of questions, not only will PCWP be normal in the setting of cor pulmonale, but it will also be elevated if there is any left heart pathology.
rapidFireQAs.a: Hypovolemic shock arrows → CO down, VR down, TPR up, PCWP down (or low-normal). Cardiogenic shock arrows → CO down, VR down, TPR up, PCWP up. Septic + anaphylactic shock arrows → CO up, VR up, TPR down, PCWP normal. Neurogenic shock + adrenal crisis arrows → CO down, VR down, TPR down, PCWP normal.

rapidFireQAs.q: 23F + non-smoker + gradually worsening shortness of breath + loud P2 + CXR shows increased pulmonary vascular markings; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: primary pulmonary hypertension → common cause is mutations in BMPR2.

rapidFireQAs.q: Treatment of pulmonary hypertension?
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE will generally not make you pick and choose between agents, however it is generally accepted in the literature that dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, such as nifedipine, are effective in vasoreactive pulmonary hypertension. Other agents include prostaglandin I2 (epoprostenol), bosentan (endothelin-1 receptor antagonist), and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil; yes, Viagra).

rapidFireQAs.q: “Am I supposed to know something about endothelin-1?”
rapidFireQAs.a: Step 1 pulmonary material has an obsession with it. Be aware that endothelin-1 is a potent vasoconstrictor → so increased endothelin-1 activity is associated with pulmonary hypertension.

rapidFireQAs.q: 23F with primary pulmonary hypertension; Q asks which of the following might be seen in this patient; answer = “increased endothelin-1 activity”
rapidFireQAs.a: essentially, if bosentan is a HY antagonist of endothelin-1 as a Tx for pulmonary hypertension, then it makes sense that increased activity is correlated with pulmonary hypertension in patients.

rapidFireQAs.q: 68M + S3 + crackles in both lungs + JVD + peripheral edema; what would be seen in this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: “increased endothelin-1 activity” → congestive heart failure is defined as right heart failure caused by left heart failure; because the lungs need to accommodate more fluid secondary to the backup from the decompensated left heart, the pulmonary vessels constrict (endothelin-1 activity) → pulmonary hypertension → right heart experiences increased afterload and then also fails.

rapidFireQAs.q: Which lung cancers are apical vs central?
rapidFireQAs.a: Central → sounds like Sentral → Squamous cell, Small cell; peripheral → adenocarcinoma, large cell.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + non-smoker + apical lung mass; no other information; most likely cancer?
rapidFireQAs.a: adenocarcinoma → classically female non-smokers with peripheral lesion, although I’ve seen it show up in a male as well on NBME.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + non-smoker + peripheral lung mass + proximal muscle weakness + increased serum CK + rash on shoulders; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: paraneoplastic dermatomyositis secondary to bronchogenic adenocarcinoma.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + non-smoker + lung mass + thrombosis; lung cancer Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: adenocarcinoma. In general, cancer is associated with hypercoagulable state, but this is particularly the case for adenocarcinomas; in addition, Trousseau sign of malignancy (migratory thrombophlebitis) is characteristic of adenocarcinomas (not limited to head of pancreas adenocarcinoma).

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + long smoking Hx + shooting groin pain; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: ureterolithiasis secondary to hypercalcemia from bronchogenic squamous cell carcinoma PTHrp (PTH related peptide) secretion.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + long smoking Hx + shooting groin pain + serum studies show high calcium; what is the patient’s PTH level?
rapidFireQAs.a: decreased (suppressed in the setting of high PTHrp).

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + dies of lung cancer + Q shows you gross pathologic specimen of large, cavitating, central lesion; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: squamous cell carcinoma → cavitations are common.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + lung cancer + Hx of stabbing flank pain a couple months ago + today presents with confusion; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: hypercalcemic crisis → squamous cell carcinoma with PTHrp secretion with Hx of nephrolithiasis; high calcium can cause delirium.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + long smoking Hx + central coin lesion on CXR + violaceous abdominal striae + potassium level of 3.0 mEq/L; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: small cell carcinoma with ectopic ACTH secretion; student says, “Wait but why’s the potassium low?” → effect of chronically high cortisol (can act to secrete K at distal kidney similar to aldosterone; only seen in ongoing Cushing syndrome).

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + confirmed Dx of early-stage small cell lung cancer + wobbly gait; Q asks the mechanism for her presentation; answer = autoimmune
rapidFireQAs.a: paraneoplastic anti-Hu and anti-Yo antibodies causing cerebellar dysfunction; Dx is small cell cerebellar dysfunction (small cell is known to cause neuronal paraneoplastic syndromes beyond Lambert-Eaton).

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + central lung lesion + confusion + increased urinary osmolality; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: SIADH secondary to small cell → low serum sodium + high urinary osmolality; should be noted that sodium derangement (high or low), as well as high calcium, can cause CNS disturbance / delirium.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + long smoking Hx + difficulty getting up from chair but is successful after multiple attempts; what is the location of her pathology?
rapidFireQAs.a: neuromuscular junction → small cell paraneoplastic Lambert-Eaton syndrome → antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F non-smoker + episodic flushing, wheezing, and dyspnea + coin lesion seen on CXR; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: bronchial carcinoid tumor.

rapidFireQAs.q: 33F + Hx of recent molar pregnancy + very high serum beta-hCG levels + new-onset non-productive cough; CXR shows multiple peripheral densities in right lobe; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: metastatic choriocarcinoma (loves to metastasize to the lungs; chorio can progress from hydatidiform mole).

rapidFireQAs.q: Do we do lung cancer screening? → Annual low-dose chest CT in patients who meet all of the following:
rapidFireQAs.a: Age 50-80. >20-pack-year Hx of smoking. Have smoked in past 15 years.

rapidFireQAs.q: 3M + swallows a peanut; where in the lung does it go? → superior segment of right lower lobe if patient is supine; goes to inferior segment of right lower lobe if patient is upright. This is because the right mainstem bronchus is shorter and straighter than the left. - “How does this type I vs II respiratory failure stuff apply more specifically to questions?” → Type I is when O2 and CO2 are both low. Type II is when O2 is low and CO2 is high.
rapidFireQAs.a: For acute asthma, the patient will have a type I respiratory failure: low pO2, low pCO2, normal bicarb, high pH → in this setting, RR is high (e.g., 28/min), so pCO2 is low, not high, because the CO2 can diffuse out with no problem; however O2 is low because the bronchospasm and secretions prevent the slow-diffusing O2 from sufficiently entering the capillary beds; bicarb is unchanged because it’s the acute setting; it will not normally start to appreciably decrease for at least 12-24 hours (just think, similarly, it takes at least a day for bicarb to decrease when one goes to high altitude, resulting in altitude sickness); pH is high because of acute respiratory alkalosis (once again, bicarb hasn’t decreased to compensate). Classic USMLE scenario for type II is asthma attack after 30-45 minutes, where the patient’s values are as follows: low pO2, normal pCO2, normal bicarb, normal pH; the Q asks what you should do: answer = intubation → reason being: the low O2 clearly means the patient is still in respiratory distress, however the rising of CO2 into the normal range (and restoration of pH to normal) indicates this is only because the patient is getting tired – i.e., RR is falling out of fatigue, not because the patient’s O2 has stabilized. In this setting, the patient is in transition to a type II respiratory failure. In other words, if we don’t intubate, the patient’s values will soon become: low pO2, high pCO2, normal bicarb, low pH (i.e., respiratory acidosis; type II respiratory failure). For pulmonary embolism, we also have a type I respiratory failure: low pO2, low pCO2, normal bicarb, high pH, same as acute asthma. Bicarb is once again unchanged because it’s the acute setting; pCO2 is low because RR is high; O2 is low because of pathologic dead space (high V/Q → despite good ventilation, reduced perfusion results in reduced arterial oxygenation). For opioids, we expect hypoventilation, so we have: low pO2, high pCO2, normal bicarb, low pH (respiratory acidosis; type II respiratory failure), secondary to the patient’s low RR.

rapidFireQAs.q: What kind of acid-base disturbance do we have in COPD exacerbation?
rapidFireQAs.a: Acute on chronic respiratory acidosis. NBME can write this as "chronic respiratory acidosis with acute respiratory acidosis." Patients with COPD are chronic CO2 retainers so will have chronic respiratory acidosis (high CO2, high bicarb to compensate, low or normal pH). Then when there is an exacerbation on top of it, CO2 will shoot even higher, where have super-high CO2, high bicarb, low pH. This can occur even if respiratory rate is high.

rapidFireQAs.q: What do I need to know about FEV1/FVC?
rapidFireQAs.a: normal ratio is considered >0.7 (according to AAFP); ratio is decreased in obstructive lung disease (<0.7; <70%); ratio is normal or increased in restrictive lung disease (>0.7; >70%). In both obstructive and restrictive, FEV1 and FVC, as independent variables, both decrease; it’s only the ratio that differs.

rapidFireQAs.q: Why is the FEV1/FVC ratio normal or increased in restrictive?
rapidFireQAs.a: typical student response is, “Well FEV1 doesn’t go down as much as FVC in restrictive.” But why is this the case? → answer that pops up all over NBME exams is radial traction → i.e., if the restrictive pathology is caused by fibrosis / scar formation, we could colloquially say that fibrosis is “sticky,” where it sticks to the outside of the airways and keeps them from closing → the amount of air one breathes out in one second (FEV1) doesn’t go down as much as it does in an obstructive lung disease, where radial traction doesn’t play a role (so FEV1 goes down even more in obstructive pathologies → FEV1/FVC is low in obstructive).

rapidFireQAs.q: 59F + advanced COPD and lung cancer + requires partial pneumonectomy + FEV1 of left lung is 600mL; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: “measurement of FEV1 of the right lung” → seemingly weird answer but HY for pulm component of surg shelves → minimum acceptable postoperative FEV1 for both lungs is 800mL.

rapidFireQAs.q: “What is obstructive vs restrictive lung disease?”
rapidFireQAs.a: obstructive lung disease means air-trapping occurs because there is literally obstruction in the airways, resulting in prolonged expiratory phase; restrictive means there is decreased ability for the lungs to expand (decreased compliance) but expiratory component remains unaffected in pure restrictive pathology.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are some common obstructive vs restrictive conditions?
rapidFireQAs.a: Obstructive: emphysema + bronchitis (combo = COPD); asthma. Restrictive: autoimmune diseases (many conditions can result in fibrosis, such as rheumatoid arthritis [rheumatoid lung], systemic sclerosis [both diffuse and limited {CREST}], sarcoidosis); Hx of radiation to the chest (i.e., Hx of Hodgkin) leading to fibrosis; pneumoconioses (asbestosis, silicosis, etc.); ankylosing spondylitis; obesity; neuromuscular disease (i.e., myasthenia gravis, Guillain-Barre).

rapidFireQAs.q: What is definition of chronic bronchitis?
rapidFireQAs.a: productive cough every day for >3 months in a year for at least two consecutive years; most common cause is smoking.

rapidFireQAs.q: 57M + 4-day Hx of productive cough + COPD managed with ipratropium inhaler + afebrile + HR 110 + RR 22 + BP 130/80 + O2 sats 90% + breath sounds decreased bilaterally + CXR shows hyperinflation of both lungs; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on NBME = “bronchitis” → i.e., acute bronchitis; usually viral.

rapidFireQAs.q: Classic way to differentiate COPD from asthma?
rapidFireQAs.a: in asthma, spirometry showing decreased respiratory function is largely reversible with albuterol; this is modestly effective at best in COPD; “flattened diaphragm” is classic CXR descriptor for hyperinflated lungs seen in COPD; this descriptor can be seen in asthma, but is rare.

rapidFireQAs.q: “What do I need to know about DLCO?”
rapidFireQAs.a: stands for diffusion capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (correct, not dioxide); test measures difference in partial pressures of inspired vs expired carbon monoxide; you just need to know that DLCO is decreased for most lung pathologies, however it is increased in asthma; how this applies to questions → if you get a hard vignette (e.g., COPD vs asthma, etc.) and they tell you DLCO is down, you can say, “Ok cool, it’s not asthma.”

rapidFireQAs.q: “What do we need to know in terms of lung volumes and flow-loop stuff for obstructive vs restrictive?
rapidFireQAs.a: in general, lung volumes are increased in obstructive lung pathologies and decreased in restrictive ones. The following diagrams illustrate some of the changes in obstructive vs restrictive lung disease:

rapidFireQAs.q: 72F + longitudinal study comparing her lung function to 20-yr-olds’ lungs; what changes would we expect in her versus young individuals?
rapidFireQAs.a: residual volume ↑; arterial pO2 ↓; A-a pO2 gradient ↑; essentially, people develop obstructive lung disease changes as they age (likely due to lifelong inhalation of particulates, akin to smoking).

rapidFireQAs.q: 38F smoker + study performed comparing her to healthy individuals; what changes would we expect in her compared to non-smokers
rapidFireQAs.a: mucous production and secretion ↑; activity of airway cilia ↓; alveolar macrophage function ↓; increased mucous production and secretion reflects changes tending toward bronchitis; activity of airway cilia decreases with exposure to particulates; this point is insidiously HY for USMLE Step 1; alveolar macrophage function and activity are impaired by particulates (even though increased clearance necessary).

rapidFireQAs.q: What is one of the most important descriptors in a Q for restrictive lung disease?
rapidFireQAs.a: reticulonodular or reticular pattern seen on CXR and CT → memorize these descriptors as = restrictive lung disease; they are also known as honeycombing colloquially.

rapidFireQAs.q: “When is centri-acinar vs pan-acinar emphysema important?”
rapidFireQAs.a: you just need to know that centri- acinar is the distribution seen in smoking; pan-acinar is seen in alpha-1 anti-trypsin deficiency.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M non-smoker + reduced lung function + has a 40-year-old brother with COPD + father died of alcoholic liver disease; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: alpha-1 anti-trypsin deficiency → enzyme is produced in liver and travels to the lungs; functions to breakdown elastase; deficiency results in pan-acinar emphysema (Q will mention non-smoker with emphysema); can also result in hepatic cirrhosis (alcohol exacerbates already poor liver prognosis); codominant inheritance.

rapidFireQAs.q: “When is bronchiectasis the answer?”
rapidFireQAs.a: when the vignette tells you “cups and cups of foul-smelling sputum”; this is how bronchiectasis presents 8 out of 10 times; there is destruction of the musculature of the bronchioles resulting in ectatic (dilated) airways → “loss of elastic support to the walls of the bronchioles” (NBME); Q might also show you a CT scan (1 out of 10 Qs) where it appears as though there’s dilated spaces throughout both lung fields; most common cause worldwide is TB; in western countries it’s CF; smoking is also ubiquitous cause; the hardest presentation is pediatrics (1 out of 10 Qs), where the Dx is “right middle lobe syndrome” → Q will say there’s a 6-12-month Hx of non-productive cough + a linear/streaky opacity seen on CXR in the right middle lobe → answer = bronchiectasis. Student will say “? I thought it was supposed to be cups and cups of sputum.” Yeah, it normally is, but now you know of another presentation.

rapidFireQAs.q: 34F + non-productive cough + CXR shows hilar nodularity; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: “non-caseating granulomas” → sarcoidosis; Tx = steroids; CXR will show bihilar lymphadenopathy; non-caseating granulomas produce 1-alpha hydroxylase, which converts inactive 25-OH-D3 into active 1,25-(OH)2- D3, leading to increased absorption of Ca and PO4 in the small bowel; Q will sometimes give PO4 in the normal range; also need to know that fecal calcium is low (asked on NBME; makes sense if you absorb it); PTH is also suppressed.

rapidFireQAs.q: Any drug that can be used to help diagnose asthma?
rapidFireQAs.a: methacholine (muscarinic agonist); will reproduce asthma Sx; never use during acute attacks.

rapidFireQAs.q: 34F + non-productive cough + CXR normal; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: “activation of mast cell” → asthma.

rapidFireQAs.q: Asthma Tx (outpatient)? → albuterol (short-acting beta-2 agonist; SABA) inhaler for immediate Mx → if insufficient, start low-dose ICS (inhaled corticosteroid) preventer → if insufficient, maximize dose of ICS preventer → if insufficient, add salmeterol inhaler (long-acting beta-2 agonist; LABA); in other words:
rapidFireQAs.a: 1) SABA; then 2) low-dose ICS; then 3) maximize dose ICS; then 4) LABA. The above order is universal. After the LABA, any number of agents can be given in any order – i.e., nedocromil, cromolyn sodium, zileuton, montelukast, zafirlukast, etc. Last resort is oral corticosteroids, however they are most effective. In other words:

rapidFireQAs.q: 12M + ongoing wheezing episodes + is on albuterol inhaler; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: add low-dose ICS.

rapidFireQAs.q: 12M + ongoing wheezing episodes + is on albuterol inhaler; what’s most likely to decrease recurrence?
rapidFireQAs.a: oral corticosteroids (student says “? I thought you said ICS was what we do next and that oral steroids are last resort” Yeah, you’re right, but they’re still most effective at decreasing recurrence. This isn’t something I’m romanticizing; this distinction is assessed on the FM NBME forms.

rapidFireQAs.q: MOA of nedocromil and cromolyn sodium?
rapidFireQAs.a: mast cell stabilizers.

rapidFireQAs.q: MOA of zileuton?
rapidFireQAs.a: lipoxygenase inhibitor (enzyme that makes leukotrienes from arachidonic acid).

rapidFireQAs.q: MOA of the -lukasts?
rapidFireQAs.a: leukotriene LTC, D, and E4 inhibitors. LTB4 receptor agonism is unrelated and induces neutrophilic chemotaxis (LTB4, IL-8, kallikrein, platelet-activating factor, C5a, bacterial proteins).

rapidFireQAs.q: 16M goes snowboarding all day + takes pain reliever for sore muscles afterward + next day develops wheezing out on the slopes again; what’s going on?
rapidFireQAs.a: took aspirin + this is Samter triad (now cumbersomely known as aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease [AERD]) → triad of aspirin- induced asthma + aspirin hypersensitivity + nasal polyps). Just to be clear, other NSAIDs can precipitate Samter triad, but the literature + USMLE will make it explicitly about aspirin.

rapidFireQAs.q: 16M takes aspirin + gets wheezing; what are we likely to see on physical exam?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on USMLE = nasal polyps.

rapidFireQAs.q: “Wait I don’t understand. Why would aspirin cause asthma?”
rapidFireQAs.a: arachidonic acid can be shunted down either the cyclooxygenase or lipoxygenase pathways; if you knock out COX irreversibly by giving aspirin (or reversibly with another NSAID), more arachidonic acid will be shunted down the lipoxygenase pathway → more leukotrienes → more bronchoconstriction.

rapidFireQAs.q: Kid has Hx of AERD; physician considers agent to decrease his recurrence of Sx
rapidFireQAs.a: zileuton, or -lukasts (both are correct; and only one will be listed).

rapidFireQAs.q: 10F + diffuse wheezes heard bilaterally + sputum sample shows numerous eosinophils and Charcot- Leyden crystals; which of the following is implicated in her disease pathogenesis?
rapidFireQAs.a: leukotriene C4 (LTC4); should be noted that LTC4, LTD4, and LTE4 all cause bronchoconstriction; LTB4 stimulates neutrophilic chemotaxis; Charcot-Leyden crystals are seen in asthma and are composed to eosinophil protein galectin-10.

rapidFireQAs.q: Any weird asthma Txs?
rapidFireQAs.a: omalizumab → monoclonal antibody against IgE → used for intractable, severe asthma unresponsive to oral steroids + in patients who have eosinophilia + high IgE levels (I asked a pulmonologist about this drug years ago when I was in MS3 and he said he was managing 1000 patients with asthma and just three were on omalizumab).

rapidFireQAs.q: Acute asthma Mx (emergencies)
rapidFireQAs.a: most important piece of info straight-up is: USMLE wants you to know that inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) have no role in acute asthma management. First thing we do is give oxygen (any USMLE Q that shows depressed O2 sats, answer is always O2) + nebulized albuterol (face mask with mist); IV steroids are then administered. The Mx algorithm is more complicated, but that is what you need for the USMLE.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25F + runny nose and eyes in spring + cobblestoning of nasal mucosa; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: allergic rhinitis (“cobblestoning” is buzz term but used on the NBME); Tx = avoidance of precipitating allergen (if known, e.g., pollen); if meds used, first-line = intranasal corticosteroids; second-line is oral or intranasal antihistamines (e.g., loratadine).

rapidFireQAs.q: 27M + inhalation injury from housefire + Q asks “destruction to which structure is most likely to preclude restoration of normal pulmonary architecture and lung function?”
rapidFireQAs.a: basement membranes → USMLE wants you to know intact basement membranes necessary for complete healing from lung injury or infection.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M alcoholic + fever + air-fluid level seen on CXR; Dx + TX?
rapidFireQAs.a: pulmonary abscess; Tx = clindamycin; air-fluid level = circle on CXR, where bottom half is pus (radiopaque; white); top half is air (radiolucent; black); due to aspiration of “oropharyngeal anaerobes” (bacteroides, Mobiluncus, Peptostreptococcus).

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M alcoholic + fever + CXR shows lobar consolidation + sputum is thick and red; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Klebsiella pneumoniae (produces thick, mucoid colonies with “currant jelly sputum”); common cause of aspiration pneumonia (increased risk in alcoholics).

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M alcoholic + fever + CXR shows lobar consolidation + extremely foul-smelling sputum; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Bacteroides pneumonia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M alcoholic + fever + air-fluid level seen on CXR + clindamycin is given and resolves his condition + months later he has residual lesion seen on CXR; why?
rapidFireQAs.a: failure of maintenance of basement membranes.

rapidFireQAs.q: Function of type I vs II pneumocytes?
rapidFireQAs.a: type I composes 95% of alveolar surface area (simple squamous) and is responsible for gas exchange; type II pneumocytes are interspersed and fewer; they produce surfactant (contain specialized surfactant-producing organelles called lamellar bodies) and also function as the stem cells of the lung (i.e., after lung injury, type II multiply and restore type I cells, insofar as basement membranes remain intact).

rapidFireQAs.q: What are Clara cells
rapidFireQAs.a: secrete glycosaminoglycans to protect the lining of bronchioles.

rapidFireQAs.q: Child born at 28 weeks gestation + dyspnea + Q asks which of the following is likely true in the patient
rapidFireQAs.a: “deficiency of lamellar bodies” → neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS); aka hyaline membrane disease → deficiency of surfactant → reduced lecithin (dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine) to sphingomyelin ratio; ratio should be >2.

rapidFireQAs.q: Child born at 28 weeks gestation + dyspnea + Q asks which of the following is likely true in the patient
rapidFireQAs.a: deficiency of surfactant protein D → need to know this is decreased in NRDS.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate born at 38 weeks gestation via C-section + RR of 70 (normal 40-60) + CXR shows bilateral mild hyperinflation and prominent perihilar interstitial markings ; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: transient tachypnea of the newborn → TTN is the answer when the vignette “sounds like NRDS but the kid is term”; seen in C-sections and fast vaginal deliveries in term neonates; mechanism is delayed absorption of the fetal lung fluid by pulmonary lymphatics; Tx is supportive.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate born at 26 weeks + required oxygen in ICU for several weeks + is now on home oxygen; child is at increased risk for what?
rapidFireQAs.a: answers = bronchopulmonary dysplasia, retinopathy of prematurity, germinal matrix bleed → all can be seen in neonates on oxygen therapy.

rapidFireQAs.q: Newborn + decreased bowel sounds in abdomen + tracheal shift to the right; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: congenital diaphragmatic hernia → incomplete formation of pleuroperitoneal membranes → occurs on the left side, with bowel herniating into the left hemithorax.

rapidFireQAs.q: Newborn + bowel sounds heard in the left chest; mechanism?
rapidFireQAs.a: incomplete formation of pleuroperitoneal membranes.

rapidFireQAs.q: 12-hour-old newborn + becomes blue when breastfeeding + becomes pink again when crying; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: atresia of the choanae (CHARGE syndrome → Coloboma of the eye, Heart defects, Atresia of the choanae, Retardation, Genitourinary abnormalities, Ear abnormalities/deafness).

rapidFireQAs.q: Can you comment on HY pneumoconioses? → lung disease secondary to occupational exposures.
rapidFireQAs.a: Asbestosis → workers in shipbuilding, plumbing, construction/insulation, roofing industries → causes supradiaphragmatic and pleural plaques; plaques can calcify; biopsy may show ferruginous bodies (due to deposition of hemosiderin by alveolar macrophages attempting to digest asbestos fibers); Step 1 NBME Q asks which cell is responsible for the pulmonary fibrosis seen in asbestosis → answer = macrophage. Anthracosis → “coalminer’s lung”; carbon deposition; black appearance grossly; also what city-dwellers may develop by old age; restrictive lung pattern on spirometry. Silicosis → stone quarry workers; eggshell calcifications; increased risk of TB due to decreased alveolar macrophage function; do not give anti-TNF-alpha agents to these patients (because they further increase risk of TB); do PPD test if new Dx of silicosis; restrictive on spirometry. Berylliosis → aeronautical industry workers; granulomatous disease, so steroids might provide benefit; steroids do not help in the other pneumoconioses. Byssinosis → pneumoconiosis caused by hemp / textile fibers. Bagassosis → pneumoconiosis caused by sugarcane (specific antigen = thermophilic Actinomycetes). Caplan syndrome → pneumoconiosis + rheumatoid arthritis (restrictive).

rapidFireQAs.q: 34M hay farmer + progressive dyspnea over many months + clubbing; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: hypersensitivity pneumonitis; can be acute, subacute, or chronic; occurs in response to various antigens, including thermophilic Actinomycetes (hay farmers; sugarcane); non-tuberculous mycobacterium (hot tub lung; on NBME); bird fancier’s lung, coffee worker’s lung, etc.; characterized by multinucleated giant cells on biopsy.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28M + asthma + recurrent lung infections + skin allergy testing shows hypersensitivity to aspergillus antigen; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA); usually seen in patients who have asthma or cystic fibrosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 34M + HIV positive + nodular density seen in right upper lobe on CXR; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: “biopsy of the mass” → Aspergilloma (fungus ball); increased risk with Hx of TB (can occupy cavities).

rapidFireQAs.q: 57M + Hx of dermatomyositis + few weeks ago had fever and pneumonia + presentation hasn’t resolved with multiple antibiotics + multiple sputum cultures are negative; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP; formerly known as bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia [BOOP]); → frequently presents as pneumonia-like presentation (i.e., fever, dyspnea) in patients with Hx of autoimmune disease like dermatomyositis or rheumatoid arthritis; CXR resembles atypical pneumonia; COP diagnosis suspected after failure of resolution with multiple Abx and negative sputum cultures; CT shows reverse-halo sign in 20%; biopsy showing Masson bodies confirms Dx; Tx = steroids. “Organizing” refers to persistence of alveolar exudates from a pneumonia that ultimately fibrose.

rapidFireQAs.q: 43F + lung transplant several months ago + declining lung function + CXR shows mild flattening of the diaphragm + CT shows air-trapping; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: bronchiolitis obliterans (constrictive bronchiolitis; “popcorn lung”); do not confuse with COP (BOOP); bronchiolitis obliterans is the answer for obstructive lung disease that progressively manifests post-lung transplant (75%) or bone marrow transplant; also associated with toxic fumes and E-cigarettes; biopsy confirms Dx; irreversible, but steroids may help.

rapidFireQAs.q: 43F + rheumatoid arthritis + progressive shortness of breath over six months + CT of chest shows reticulonodular pattern; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: “usual interstitial pneumonia” (UIP); student says ? → on the NBME; this Dx refers to a patient with scarring and fibrosis of the lungs; if the cause is idiopathic, we call the UIP “idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis,” but IPF is still UIP. Bottom line is: be aware of the term “usual interstitial pneumonia” as synonymous with pulmonary fibrosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Drugs causing pulmonary fibrosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: methotrexate (patients with RA who have UIP → hard to know whether it’s from the methotrexate or rheumatoid lung, or both); amiodarone, bleomycin, busulfan, nitrofurantoin.

rapidFireQAs.q: 10-month-old + fever of 101F + wheezes bilaterally; DX + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: RSV bronchiolitis → Tx is supportive; answers such as ribavirin and palivizumab are almost always wrong on actual NBME assessment.

rapidFireQAs.q: 8M + leaning forward in tripod position + drooling; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: epiglottitis caused by Haemophilus influenzae type B; Tx = immediate intubation; neck x-ray shows thumbprint sign; even if kid is stable, still intubate (airway can inflame + obstruct at any moment); give ceftriaxone to patient; give rifampin to close contacts; usually seen in immigrants due to lack of adequate vaccination.

rapidFireQAs.q: 8M + hoarse cough + improves when father brings him out in the cold; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) caused by parainfluenza virus (paramyxovirus); classically “seal-like, barking cough”; neck x-ray shows steeple sign (subglottic narrowing); Tx = supportive; if you’re forced to pick an actual Tx however, choose “nebulized racemic epinephrine.”

rapidFireQAs.q: 8M + two weeks ago recovered from influenza infection + now has fever + inspiratory stridor + can open mouth fully; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: bacterial tracheitis caused by Staph aureus. Dx with bronchoscopy; Tx with antibiotics. Being able to open the mouth fully is important detail, since with peritonsillar abscess, one has difficulty opening the mouth fully. If a patient has recently recovered from a viral URTI, S. aureus secondary infections are a HY possible sequela.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40M + 6-month Hx of episodic sinusitis + cough with blood-tinged sputum + no improvement of Sx after several months of antibiotics, decongestants, and nasal corticosteroids + P/E shows two small ulcerations on nasal mucosa; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly known as Churg-Strauss) → presents as asthma-like Sx and eosinophilia in a patient with positivity for p-ANCA (anti-myeloperoxidase; anti-MPO); overlap of features with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly known as Wegener, which is c-ANCA [anti-proteinase 3; anti-PR3]).

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M + hemoptysis + hematuria + ANCA screen is negative; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: anti- glomerular basement membrane antibody screen → Dx likely Goodpasture; if anti-GBM antibodies positive, do renal biopsy showing linear immunofluorescence; anti-GBM Abs = antibodies against type IV collagen (“2, 3, 4; 2, 3, 4; 2, 3, 4 – The Goodpasture is marching in the field! - 2, 3, 4; 2, 3, 4; 2, 3, 4” → type II sensitivity against the alpha-3 chains of type IV collagen).

rapidFireQAs.q: How to Dx TB?
rapidFireQAs.a: PPD skin test is performed first diagnostically. If history of BCG vaccine, do interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) instead. Do not do IGRA in addition to PPD. If PPD is negative, repeat after one week. If negative again, no further studies indicated. Repeats performed within 1 week may cause a false (+) secondary to a "booster reaction." If IGRA is negative, no further studies indicated. If PPD or IGRA is positive, do CXR. Do not repeat positive PPD tests. If CXR is negative, treat for latent TB / give TB prophylaxis. On the USMLE, "treatment for latent TB" and "administer TB prophylaxis" mean the same thing. If CXR is positive, treat for active TB.

rapidFireQAs.q: How to manage a positive PPD test?
rapidFireQAs.a: Measure induration only. Erythema does not count.

rapidFireQAs.q: 5+ mm
rapidFireQAs.a: Recent contact with people with active TB HIV + status Organ transplant recipients Chronic prednisone use (>15mg/day for >1 month); anti-TNF-α agent use Findings consistent with TB on CXR

rapidFireQAs.q: 10+ mm
rapidFireQAs.a: Immigrant status (Western countries not included) IV drug users Healthcare workers; prison workers; homeless shelter personnel TB laboratory personnel Children under 4 years of age

rapidFireQAs.q: 15+ mm
rapidFireQAs.a: Everyone

rapidFireQAs.q: How to Tx latent TB?
rapidFireQAs.a: 9 months INH + pyridoxine (vitamin B6) - The USMLE USMLE Step 1 assess this as the answer. 4 months rifampin 3 months INH + rifapentine + pyridoxine Vitamin B6 must be given with INH to prevent vitamin B6 deficiency.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of active TB
rapidFireQAs.a: Rifampin, INH, pyrazinamide, ethambutol (RIPE) for 2 months, followed by RI alone for 4 more months (6 months total) And of course add pyridoxine (annoying that it sounds similar to pyrazinamide)

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + fever of 101F + CXR shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Mycoplasma pneumoniae; most common cause of atypical pneumonia after viruses; classically bilateral.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + fever 101F + CXR shows lobar consolidation + dullness to percussion on P/E; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Streptococcus pneumoniae → need to know is gram-positive diplococci (don’t confuse with Neisseria gonorrhea and meningitides, which are gram-negative diplococci).

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + fever 101F + CXR shows lobar consolidation with interstitial markings; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Mycoplasma → likely implication is that even though Strep pneumo is classically lobar and Mycoplasma bilateral, if the Q says the word “interstitial,” that wins over distribution/location.

rapidFireQAs.q: Pneumonia + diarrhea + hyponatremia; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Legionella pneumophila.

rapidFireQAs.q: Pneumonia in a cattle farmer; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Coxiella burnetti.

rapidFireQAs.q: Pneumonia in someone with a pet rabbit; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Francisella tularensis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Pneumonia in bird owner; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Chlamydia psittaci.

rapidFireQAs.q: Pneumonia in 2-week-old neonate who had ophthalmia neonatorum treated a week ago; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia → chlamydial neonatal conjunctivitis → drains through nasolacrimal duct into nasopharynx and into the lung.

rapidFireQAs.q: Pneumonia in someone who recently recovered from viral infection (usually flu); Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Staph aureus → similar to post-viral bacterial tracheitis caused by Staph.

rapidFireQAs.q: Lobar pneumonia in HIV patient; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Strep pneumo, not Pneumocystis.

rapidFireQAs.q: HIV patient + CXR shows bilateral ground-glass pneumonia; next best step in Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: bronchoalveolar lavage with silver-staining of the yeast; Dx? → Pneumocystis jirovecii → Tx = TMP/SMX.

rapidFireQAs.q: Empiric Tx for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP)?
rapidFireQAs.a: azithromycin (macrolide) → covers atypicals (i.e., Mycoplasma, etc.) and S. pneumo.

rapidFireQAs.q: Empiric Tx for CAP when patient’s had antibiotics in the past three months?
rapidFireQAs.a: respiratory fluoroquinolone (i.e., levofloxacin).

rapidFireQAs.q: When is pneumonia considered hospital-acquired (HAP)?
rapidFireQAs.a: if Sx start >48 hours after admission to hospital.

rapidFireQAs.q: How is HAP and ventilator-acquired pneumonia (VAP) Tx differently from CAP?
rapidFireQAs.a: need to cover MRSA and Pseudomonas just in case → Tx entails various broad-spectrum options; classics are vancomycin + third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin; ceftazidime (3rd gen ceph) and cefepime (4th gen ceph) are effective against Pseudomonas; piperacillin/tazobactam (“PipTaz”) is classic combo; amikacin (aminoglycoside) is effective against Pseudomonas; ceftaroline and ceftobiprole are 5th gen cephs effective against MRSA; meropenem (or imipenem/cilastatin) also used for HAP/VAP.

rapidFireQAs.q: When to do home oxygen therapy in COPD?
rapidFireQAs.a: when patient’s arterial pO2 <55 mmHg (or <60 mmHg if patient has cor pulmonale).

rapidFireQAs.q: 55M with COPD; number-one way to decrease mortality?
rapidFireQAs.a: smoking cessation; if patient has already stopped smoking, answer = home oxygen therapy (decreases mortality, but only indicated as per criteria above).

rapidFireQAs.q: 48M + BMI 45 + snores loudly during sleep; what is most likely seen in this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: increased serum bicarbonate → Dx = obesity hypoventilation syndrome → blood levels of CO2 are increased, with bicarb increased to compensate (chronic respiratory acidosis).

rapidFireQAs.q: 8-month-old girl + stridor that improves with neck extension; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: vascular ring → weird but HY diagnosis for peds → aberrant embryologic development where the aorta and/or surrounding vessels form a ring around the esophagus and/or trachea.

rapidFireQAs.q: 8-month-old girl + stridor that improves when prone or upright; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: laryngomalacia → most common cause of stridor in peds → soft cartilage of upper larynx collapses during inhalation.

rapidFireQAs.q: 2F + stridor + laryngoscopy shows small growths of larynx; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: HPV 6/11 → laryngeal papillomatosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Highest yield points about cystic fibrosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: autosomal recessive; chromosome 7; CFTR gene; codes for chloride channel that functions to secrete chloride in the lungs and pancreas, and reabsorb chloride in the sweat glands; DF508 (deletion of phenylalanine at position 508) is most common mutation; sweat chloride test >60 mEq/L is most diagnostic (more than genotyping); mutated CFTR channel is usually retained in rough endoplasmic reticulum in the cytosol (i.e., doesn’t make it to cell surface); disease causes a negative transepithelial potential difference (TEPD) across nasal epithelium; neonates can be screened with a positive blood immunoreactive trypsinogen; Pseudomonas eclipses S. aureus as most common cause of pneumonia after age 10; before age 10, S. aureus eclipses Pseudomonas; male infertility due to congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens (CBAVD); various Txs exist, however a couple to be aware of: dornase-alfa is a deoxyribonuclease that can help reduce the viscosity of mucous secretions; Ivacaftor is a CFTR potentiator that helps restore function of the misfolded protein.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + Hx of recurrent lung infections + two years of inability to have children with wife + wife has two children from prior marriage + his sperm sample shows immotile sperm; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Kartagener syndrome (primary ciliary dyskinesia) → dynein arm defect of cilia (a cilium on cross- section has a 9x2 arrangement of microtubules); associated with dextrocardia / situs inversus; sperm are immotile (require cilia function); this contrasts with CF, which has no sperm in the sample due to CBAVD.

rapidFireQAs.q: What should I know about breath sounds, percussion, tracheal shift, etc.?
rapidFireQAs.a: Basically all of that annoying physical exam stuff.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Pleural effusion in someone who has pneumonia; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: parapneumonic effusion (exudative pleural effusion secondary to a lung infection).

rapidFireQAs.q: What is empyema?
rapidFireQAs.a: pus in a preexisting cavity (i.e., refers to pus in the pleural space); in contrast, an abscess is pus in a location where there was not a preexisting cavity (e.g., the forearm).

rapidFireQAs.q: Characteristic of parapneumonic effusion most predictive of progression to empyema?
rapidFireQAs.a: decreased pH of the pleural fluid (<7.1).

rapidFireQAs.q: Transudative vs exudative pleural effusion? → Light’s criteria for exudative:
rapidFireQAs.a: Pleural fluid to serum protein ratio >0.5, OR Pleural fluid to serum LDH ratio >0.6, OR Pleural fluid LDH > 2/3 upper limit of serum LDH.

rapidFireQAs.q: Any other characteristics notable for transudative vs exudative?
rapidFireQAs.a: qualitatively, in exudative, pleural fluid cell count will be higher than in transudative; glucose can also be reduced in infective causes (parapneumonic).

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M + long Hx of smoking + dullness to percussion 2/3 up the lung field; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: malignant pleural effusion → malignancy, congestive heart failure, and infection are very common causes of pleural effusion.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + ovarian fibroma + ascites + hydrothorax; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Meig syndrome.

rapidFireQAs.q: Treatment for pulmonary embolism?
rapidFireQAs.a: heparin before spiral CT of the chest; if pregnant, do V/Q scan instead of CT (sufficient for USMLE).

rapidFireQAs.q: When is IVC filter the answer for pulmonary embolism? → if the patient gets a PE while already on anticoagulation (warfarin, dabigatran, etc.) and the spiral CT has already been performed. In other words:
rapidFireQAs.a: 58F on warfarin + gets PE; next best step? → answer = CT. 58F on warfarin + gets PE + CT confirms Dx; next best step? → answer = IVC filter.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + plays basketball + few hours of shortness of breath; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: spontaneous pneumothorax caused by ruptured subapical bleb; Tx = needle decompression followed by chest tube (some small pneumothoraces can be observed, but on USMLE always Tx).

rapidFireQAs.q: 32M + MVA + dyspnea + low BP + breath sounds decreased on left + tracheal shift to right; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: tension pneumothorax; Tx = needle decompression followed by chest tube.

rapidFireQAs.q: “Cephalization of pulmonary vasculature”; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: pulmonary edema → important description that shows up in NBME vignettes → due to increased hydrostatic pressure from left heart pathology.

rapidFireQAs.q: 36M + long-bone fractures + petechiae on the chest; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: fat embolism.

rapidFireQAs.q: Motor vehicle accident (MVA) + paradoxical breathing (chest moves outward with exhalation; inward with inhalation); Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: flail chest.

rapidFireQAs.q: MVA + rib fractures + underlying infiltrates in lung + low O2 sats; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: pulmonary contusion.

rapidFireQAs.q: MVA + no rib fractures + non-central chest pain + pulmonary infiltrates underlying the painful area; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: pulmonary contusion (resources will say “white out of the lung” for pulmonary contusion, but this is buzzywordy and never shows up on actual NBME material).

rapidFireQAs.q: MVA + pulmonary infiltrates + low O2 sats + bolus of normal saline given, resulting in worsening of O2 sats; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: pulmonary contusion (contused lung is very sensitive to fluid overload).

rapidFireQAs.q: MVA + bruising/pain over the sternum +/- rib fractures; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: myocardial contusion.

rapidFireQAs.q: Important point about Mx of myocardial contusion?
rapidFireQAs.a: do troponins + must monitor for arrhythmia.

rapidFireQAs.q: Adult male + abdo pain + Hx of alcohol use + diffuse pulmonary infiltrates + low O2 sats; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: ARDS → must have pO2/FiO2 <300; if the Q asks about ventilator settings, know that low- tidal volume mechanical ventilation is often used (prevents barotrauma) + permissive hypercapnia + prone positioning.

rapidFireQAs.q: When you get a random ventilator Q and they want an answer?
rapidFireQAs.a: “increase PEEP” almost always right.

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient has improving O2 sats on ventilator; next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: “wean from ventilator. ”

rapidFireQAs.q: How to differentiate viral from bacterial upper respiratory tract infection (URTI)? → CENTOR criteria:
rapidFireQAs.a: If 0 or 1 point, the URTI is unlikely to be bacterial (i.e., it’s likely to be viral). If 2-4 points, chance is much greater that URTI is bacterial. 1) Absence of cough (i.e., no cough = 1 point; if patient has cough = 0 points). 2) Fever. 3) Tonsillar exudates. 4) Lymphadenopathy (cervical, submandibular, etc.).

rapidFireQAs.q: There is a version of the criteria that includes age, but on the USMLE it can cause you to get questions wrong. So just use the simplified above four points.
rapidFireQAs.a: If 0-1 point, answer = “supportive care”; or “no treatment necessary”; or “warm saline gargle” (same as supportive care); or “acetaminophen.” Latter is answer for 3M with viral URTI + fever on Peds NBME form 2. If 0-2 points, next best step = “rapid Strep test.” If rapid Strep test is negative, answer = throat culture, NOT sputum culture. While waiting on the throat culture results, we send the patient home with amoxicillin or penicillin for presumptive Strep pharyngitis. If child is, e.g., 12 years old, and develops a rash with the beta-lactam, answer = beta-lactam allergy. If the vignette is of a 16-17 year-old who has been going on dates recently (there will be no confusion; the USMLE will make it clear), the answer = EBV mononucleosis; therefore do a heterophile antibody test (Monospot test). EBV is the odd virus out that usually presents with all four (+) CENTOR criteria. This is why it’s frequently misdiagnosed as Strep pharyngitis. It is HY to know that beta- lactams given to patients with EBV may cause rash via a hypersensitivity response to the Abx in the setting of antibody production to the virus. EBV, in a patient who does not receive Abx, can cause a mild maculopapular rash. But the rash with beta-lactam + EBV causes a more intense pruritic response generally 7-10 days following Abx administration on the extensor surfaces + pressure points.

rapidFireQAs.q: Which parameters shift the Hb-O2 dissociation curve to the right?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↑ temperature; ↑ 2,3-BPG; CO2; ↓ pH; ↑ H+ → right-shift means increased oxygen unloading at tissues; protons in the blood are buffered by deoxygenated hemoglobin (Step 1 NBME).

rapidFireQAs.q: 50M + arterial pO2 normal + arterial O2 content low; why the latter?
rapidFireQAs.a: anemia; arterial O2 content = amount of O2 dissolved in blood (pO2) + amount of O2 bound to Hb (Hb saturation); if pO2 is normal, then it should be able to bind to Hb just fine; therefore likely way O2 content is still low is if Hb levels are low (anemia). HY PULMONARY

rapidFireQAs.q: Community-acquired pneumonia (CPP) + bilateral CXR infiltrates
rapidFireQAs.a: Mycoplasma

rapidFireQAs.q: CPP + lobar pattern (right-lower lobe consolidation + dullness to percussion)
rapidFireQAs.a: Strep pneumo

rapidFireQAs.q: Pneumonia in CF patient <10 years
rapidFireQAs.a: S. aureus exceeds Pseudomonas

rapidFireQAs.q: Pneumonia in CF patient >10 years
rapidFireQAs.a: Pseudomonas exceeds S. aureus.

rapidFireQAs.q: Pneumonia after influenza infection
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE wants S. aureus

rapidFireQAs.q: Pneumonia + rabbits
rapidFireQAs.a: F. tularensis

rapidFireQAs.q: Pneumonia + cattle
rapidFireQAs.a: Coxiella (Q fever)

rapidFireQAs.q: Pneumonia + birds
rapidFireQAs.a: Chlamydia psittaci

rapidFireQAs.q: Leg swelling + pain + shortness of breath
rapidFireQAs.a: Pulmonary embolism caused by DVT

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of PE
rapidFireQAs.a: Heparin before spiral CT

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of PE in pregnant woman
rapidFireQAs.a: V/Q scan, not CT

rapidFireQAs.q: Acid-base disturbance in PE
rapidFireQAs.a: resp. alkalosis (low CO2, high pH, low O2, normal bicarb [too acute to change])

rapidFireQAs.q: Acid-base disturbance in asthma
rapidFireQAs.a: resp. alkalosis (low CO2, high pH, low O2, normal bicarb [too acute to change])

rapidFireQAs.q: Acid-base disturbance in aspirin toxicity first 20 mins
rapidFireQAs.a: resp. alkalosis (low CO2, high pH, normal O2, normal bicarb [too acute to change])

rapidFireQAs.q: Pleural / supradiaphragmatic plaques
rapidFireQAs.a: asbestosis

rapidFireQAs.q: Dry cough in winter
rapidFireQAs.a: cough-variant asthma (1/3 of asthmatics only have cough)

rapidFireQAs.q: Young African American woman + dry cough + normal CXR
rapidFireQAs.a: asthma (activation of mast cells), not sarcoidosis

rapidFireQAs.q: Young African American woman + dry cough + nodularity on CXR
rapidFireQAs.a: sarcoidosis (noncaseating granulomas)

rapidFireQAs.q: Outpatient Tx of asthma
rapidFireQAs.a: SABA, then low-dose ICS, then maximize dose of ICS, then LABA, then use any number of drugs (e.g., mast cell stabilizers, anti-leukotriene, etc.), then oral steroids last resort

rapidFireQAs.q: Kid with asthma on SABA inhaler + not effective + next best step?
rapidFireQAs.a: ICS (fluticasone)

rapidFireQAs.q: Kid with asthma on SABA inhaler + most effective way to decrease recurrence?
rapidFireQAs.a: oral steroids (not next best step, but certainly most effective)

rapidFireQAs.q: Asthma + eosinophilia
rapidFireQAs.a: Churg-Strauss

rapidFireQAs.q: Simple fungal pneumonia
rapidFireQAs.a: fluconazole

rapidFireQAs.q: Bullous changes on CXR or expanded lungs / hyperlucency
rapidFireQAs.a: emphysema

rapidFireQAs.q: Centri-acinar emphysema
rapidFireQAs.a: smokers

rapidFireQAs.q: Pan-acinar emphysema
rapidFireQAs.a: alpha-1 anti-trypsin deficiency

rapidFireQAs.q: Young adult + non-smoker + has emphysema + relative died of hepatic cirrhosis
rapidFireQAs.a: alpha-1 anti-trypsin deficiency

rapidFireQAs.q: Restrictive lung disease
rapidFireQAs.a: normal or increased FEV1/FVC

rapidFireQAs.q: Obstructive lung disease
rapidFireQAs.a: decreased FEV1/FVC

rapidFireQAs.q: Why is FEV1/FVC normal or high in restrictive?
rapidFireQAs.a: radial traction on outside of airways is sticky (keeps airways from closing)

rapidFireQAs.q: Methotrexate side-effects
rapidFireQAs.a: pulmonary fibrosis + hepatotoxicity + mouth ulcers (neutropenia)

rapidFireQAs.q: Aspiration pneumonia or pulmonary abscess; which antibiotic should be given?
rapidFireQAs.a: clindamycin (anaerobes above the diaphragm)

rapidFireQAs.q: Cups and cups of foul-smelling sputum in COPD, TB, or CF patient
rapidFireQAs.a: bronchiectasis

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common cause of bronchiectasis
rapidFireQAs.a: worldwide: TB; in western countries: CF

rapidFireQAs.q: Young kid + scant white sputum + linear opacity in right-middle lobe on CXR; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: bronchiectasis caused by right middle lobe syndrome

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M + Hx of three bacterial pneumonias + atopy; presents today with a sore left cheek; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: IgA deficiency (student says “?”) → firstly, sore cheek is sinusitis → IgA deficiency is recurrent sinopulmonary infections that “aren’t that bad” in a patient “not that young” (that is, it’s not a super- sick three-year-old like in SCID or Bruton) → can present with autoimmune phenomena like atopy and vitiligo); also can present with Hx of Giardia → apparently Step 1 is also now testing that IgA deficiency means in the Dx of Celiac disease can’t do IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase reliably bc clearly the pt wouldn’t make the IgA → anaphylaxis after blood transfusion is super HY for IgA deficiency, but also too easy and not mentioned in most Qs.

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of PJPneumonia
rapidFireQAs.a: bronchoalveolar lavage

rapidFireQAs.q: When to add steroids to TMP/SMX for PJP?
rapidFireQAs.a: A-a gradient >35 or pO2 <60 mm Hg

rapidFireQAs.q: Adult male + abdo pain + Hx of alcohol use + diffuse pulmonary infiltrates + low O2 sats
rapidFireQAs.a: ARDS

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of ARDS
rapidFireQAs.a: low-tidal volume mechanical ventilation (prevents barotrauma) + increase PEEP

rapidFireQAs.q: Asthma (outpatient)
rapidFireQAs.a: albuterol (short-acting beta-2 agonist; SABA) inhaler for immediate Mx → if insufficient, start low-dose ICS (inhaled corticosteroid) preventer → if insufficient, maximize dose of ICS preventer → if insufficient, add salmeterol inhaler (long-acting beta-2 agonist; LABA); in other words:

rapidFireQAs.q: Kid has Hx of AERD; what agent is most likely to decrease his recurrence of Sx
rapidFireQAs.a: oral steroids. We simply don’t want to give them because of their nasty side-effects (Cushing syndrome).

rapidFireQAs.q: Acid-base disturbance in asthma?
rapidFireQAs.a: respiratory alkalosis → low O2, low CO2, high pH, normal bicarb

rapidFireQAs.q: “19 times out of 20? Then what’s the exception.”
rapidFireQAs.a: I’ve seen COPD questions where the patient will have a RR of 28 but a super-high CO2, and the answer is chronic respiratory acidosis + acute respiratory acidosis (acute on chronic) → in the event of emphysema, where you literally have reduced surface area for gas exchange, even if your RR is high, CO2 has no way of diffusing out.

rapidFireQAs.q: 12M + acute asthma episode + given O2 + nebulized albuterol + IV steroids + his acid-base disturbance is as we talked about above
rapidFireQAs.a: after 30 minutes, new values are: low O2, normal CO2, normal pH, normal bicarb; why? → he’s getting tired → low O2 means he should still be hyperventilating, so for CO2 and pH to have normalized means his RR is decreasing → answer on USMLE = intubate. When O2 and CO2 are both initially down, that’s called a type I respiratory failure; then eventually it will invert, where this patient will have a respiratory acidosis with low O2, high CO2, low pH, normal bicarb (type II respiratory failure when O2 and CO2 are the opposite).

rapidFireQAs.q: Acid-base disturbance in pulmonary embolism?
rapidFireQAs.a: same as acute asthma: low O2, low CO2, high pH, normal bicarb.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of pulmonary embolism
rapidFireQAs.a: heparin before spiral CT; do V/Q scan in pregnant women.

rapidFireQAs.q: What about tPA in PE?
rapidFireQAs.a: Never an answer on the USMLE because the indications are debated.

rapidFireQAs.q: Type I HS
rapidFireQAs.a: fast-onset; anaphylaxis; atopy (asthma, hay fever [rhinoconjunctivitis], eczema); two IgEs bind antigen at Fab fragments + move into close proximity and crosslink → mast cell degranulates + secretes histamine; answer for drug rashes that occur soon after receiving the drug (e.g., sulfa); treat anaphylaxis with IM epinephrine (beta 2 agonism opens the lungs; NE doesn’t act on beta 2)

rapidFireQAs.q: Blood transfusion + dyspnea + hypoxemia + bilateral pulmonary infiltrates; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: TRALI (transfusion related acute lung injury)

rapidFireQAs.q: What causes TRALI?
rapidFireQAs.a: donor Abs against recipient MHCs → activated neutrophils cause alveolar damage → most common cause of transfusion-associated death

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient takes medication for muscle pain relief + gets wheezing (which should be avoided, acetaminophen or aspirin; both are listed)
rapidFireQAs.a: aspirin (aspirin-induced asthma)

rapidFireQAs.q: HIV patient with lobar pneumonia (is the answer PJP or S. pnuemo?)
rapidFireQAs.a: Strep pneumo → PJP presents as bilateral interstitial infiltrates + groundglass appearance on CXR; S. pneumo is lobar → sort of a trick Q similar to asbestos (i.e., bronchogenic carcinoma still more likely than mesothelioma in pt with Hx of asbestos exposure; well S. pneumo still more common than PJP in immunocompromised pts). The key though is the lobar vs bilateral presentation as mentioned above.

rapidFireQAs.q: Biochemical disturbance in aspirin toxicity in first 20 minutes: normal O2, low CO2, high pH, normal bicarb
rapidFireQAs.a: respiratory alkalosis only

rapidFireQAs.q: Severe skin infection involving fascial planes + cutaneous crepitus; organism?
rapidFireQAs.a: Clostridrium perfringens causing necrotizing fasciitis (polymicrobial, but the C. perfringens causes the gas gangrene leading to cutaneous emphysema / crepitus).

rapidFireQAs.q: 54M + progressive shortness of breath for four months + ascites + edema of lower extremities + bilateral pleural effusions + ejection fraction of 55%; what’s the mechanism for this patient’s increased fluid in the lungs?
rapidFireQAs.a: decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure (decreased plasma oncotic pressure); this refers to either renal (nephrotic syndrome) or hepatic disease (decreased production of albumin); wrong answer is “increased capillary hydrostatic pressure” because ejection fraction is normal (55-70); this is normally the answer for pulmonary edema from left heart failure; “increased vascular permeability” would be the correct answer in ARDS (bilateral pulmonary infiltrates), infection (i.e., pneumonia +/- sepsis), or pulmonary embolism (local inflammation).

rapidFireQAs.q: 15M + skiing accident + tachycardia + tachypnea + BP 98/72 + decreased breath sounds on right + CXR shows decreased lung markings on one side and large, black pleural space; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: tension pneumothorax; blood pressure can be low or low-normal; tension pneumothorax is a pneumothorax in which hemodynamic decompensation occurs (i.e., low BP); in this patient, although BP is technically low-normal, this is only because the HR is increased to compensate, and the patient will likely continue to decompensate. Mechanism for low BP in tension pneumothorax is compression of venous structures returning blood to right atrium; Q need not mention contralateral tracheal deviation; breath sounds will be decreased on affected side because air does not move in and out through the pleural space; Tx is needle decompression followed by chest tube connected to underwater apparatus.

rapidFireQAs.q: 42F + in hospital for surgery two days ago + shortness of breath + HR 92 + ECG shows no abnormalities; the medication she needs has what MOA?
rapidFireQAs.a: activation of anti-thrombin; heparin is drug given; diagnosis is pulmonary embolism; sinus tachycardia is most common finding on ECG (normal ECG + ↑ HR = sinus tachycardia); after heparin, do spiral CT of chest for diagnosis; do V/Q scan first in pregnant women.

rapidFireQAs.q: 13F + asthma attack + tremor + albuterol + IV steroids given for acute asthma attack; why is there tremor?
rapidFireQAs.a: albuterol; tremor is most common side-effect of beta-2 agonists like albuterol.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate born at 28 weeks gestation + difficulty breathing; what is deficient in this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: lamellar bodies; lamellar bodies are specialized organelles within type II pneumocytes that produce surfactant; dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (lecithin) / sphingomyelin ratio should be >2.0-2.4 for NRDS probability to be substantially decreased; elastic recoil is increased in NRDS due to lack of surfactant; surfactant normally prevents the hydrostatic forces of the alveoli from causing collapse.

rapidFireQAs.q: 30F + pancreatitis + ARDS; following complete resolution of the ARDS, what is most likely to be increased in this patient’s lungs?
rapidFireQAs.a: surfactant protein D (marker of lung injury); weird, but know it because it’s on Step 1 NBME. HY USMLE REVIEW PART IV

rapidFireQAs.q: 50M + being treated for Hodgkin + develops progressive dry cough + CXR shows reticulonodular pattern; what is most likely risk factor for this acute presentation
rapidFireQAs.a: bleomycin causing pulmonary fibrosis; reticular, or reticulonodular, or bilateral granular patterning = “honeycombing” = HY for pulmonary fibrosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M + worked in shipyard 20 years ago part-time + 6-month history of shortness of breath; CXR shows supra-diaphragmatic soft tissue densities; Q wants diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: asbestosis; risk factor is working in construction involving insulation, or shipyards; pleural and supra-diaphragmatic plaques are HY for asbestosis; mesothelioma will present as grossly white cancer that circumferentially envelopes the lungs.

rapidFireQAs.q: 66M + worked in aerospace industry for 30 years + 1-year Hx of declining pulmonary function; biopsy of lung parenchyma shows non-caseating granulomas; Q asks diagnosis
rapidFireQAs.a: berylliosis; risk factor is working in aeronautical industry; this is one of the three HY lung conditions causing granulomas (sarcoidosis + berylliosis are both non-caseating; TB is caseating).

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + smoked for 5 years + loud P2 heart sound + JVD + bullous changes seen on CXR + father died of alcoholic cirrhosis; Q wants risk factor for this patient’s condition
rapidFireQAs.a: “deficiency of neutrophil elastase”; diagnosis is cor pulmonale due to COPD from a1-antitrypsin deficiency; latter leads to pan-acinar emphysema (bullous changes on CXR are buzzy/HY for emphysema); can also cause cirrhosis; vignettes can absolutely mention smoking or alcohol Hx, where patients are at increased/accelerated risk for emphysema and cirrhosis (i.e., 5 years is too fast typically for COPD to develop). The loud P2 means pulmonary hypertension. JVD means we have right heart failure. Since the etiology of the right heart failure is pulmonary (i.e., not left heart), we call it cor pulmonale.

rapidFireQAs.q: 36F + new-onset shortness of breath and tachycardia; patient has 5-pack-year Hx of smoking + recently prescribed combined oral contraceptive pill; Q asks which of the following would have prevented this patient’s acute presentation
rapidFireQAs.a: avoidance of combined contraceptives; diagnosis is pulmonary embolism; combined contraceptives (i.e., containing estrogen in addition to progesterone in order to minimize breakthrough bleeding) are contraindicated in women 35+ who are smokers. They are also contraindicated in women who have migraines with aura, active breast cancer, or Hx of thromboembolic disease. This is because estrogen-containing contraception (and HRT) increases risk of thromboembolic events (estrogen upregulates fibrinogen and factors V and VIII).

rapidFireQAs.q: 8F + long Hx of recurrent pulmonary infections + 6-month history of peripheral neuropathy; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: cystic fibrosis resulting in vitamin E deficiency (can present as neuropathy). This sounds low-yield and weird, but it’s all over the NBME exams for Step 1 (i.e., vitamin E deficiency due to CF).

rapidFireQAs.q: 60F + low serum sodium + concentrated urine + history of weight loss; Dx + risk factor?
rapidFireQAs.a: SIADH due to small cell lung cancer; smoking is risk factor.
